overview.title: From NumPy to Keras: the SimpleRNN layer and return_sequences
overview.main_topic: The Keras SimpleRNN layer as the batched version of the NumPy RNN; variable-length inputs via timesteps=None; the two output modes controlled by return_sequences
overview.central_idea: SimpleRNN implements the loop of p.391 on batches of shape (batch_size, timesteps, input_features). Setting timesteps to None allows arbitrary sequence lengths, and return_sequences chooses between returning every timestep's output (rank 3) or only the last one (rank 2, the default).
overview.importance: Knowing the input and output shapes of recurrent layers, and when to return full sequences, is required to build any recurrent model, including the stacked and bidirectional models later in this chapter.
learning_objectives: Explain why the last RNN output can summarize the whole sequence
State the input shape expected by Keras recurrent layers
Use keras.Input(shape=(None, num_features)) for variable-length sequences and know the trade-offs
Distinguish return_sequences=True and False and their output shapes
Predict the output shape of SimpleRNN(16) on an input of shape (None, 120, 14)
prerequisites: The NumPy simple RNN of pp.390-391
The Jena dataset's 14 features and 120-step windows (section 13.2)

summary:
The page opens with a **NOTE** closing section 13.3.1: in the NumPy example the final output is a rank-2 tensor of shape `(timesteps, output_features)` in which the output at each timestep `t` carries information about input timesteps `0` to `t`, the entire past. Hence often you need only the **last output**, which already contains information about the whole sequence.

**Section 13.3.2** maps the NumPy loop to the Keras **`SimpleRNN`** layer. The one minor difference: like all Keras layers, `SimpleRNN` processes **batches** of sequences, taking inputs of shape `(batch_size, timesteps, input_features)` rather than `(timesteps, input_features)`. In `keras.Input(shape=...)` the `timesteps` entry may be `None`, letting the network process sequences of **arbitrary length**. **Listing 13.16** shows this with `num_features = 14` and `layers.SimpleRNN(16)`.

The authors add that variable length is useful when your sequences actually vary; if they all have the same length, they recommend a complete input shape, because `model.summary()` can then display output lengths and some **performance optimizations** become possible (sidebar "On RNN runtime performance" in section 13.3.4, on p.398).

Finally, all Keras recurrent layers (`SimpleRNN`, `LSTM`, `GRU`) have **two output modes**, selected by the constructor argument **`return_sequences`**:

- full sequence of outputs: rank-3 tensor `(batch_size, timesteps, output_features)`;
- only the last output: rank-2 tensor `(batch_size, output_features)`.

**Listing 13.17** builds an input of shape `(120, 14)` and applies `SimpleRNN(16, return_sequences=False)`; printing the output shape gives `(None, 16)`. The callout notes that `return_sequences=False` is the **default**. The full-sequence variant follows on p.393.

paragraphs.excerpt: NOTE In this example, the final output is a rank-2 tensor of shape
paragraphs.what_it_says: In the NumPy example the final output has shape (timesteps, output_features); each timestep's output contains information about input timesteps 0 to t. So in many cases you need only the last output, which contains information about the entire sequence.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because the state is threaded through every step, output_t is a function of x_0..x_t. The last output is therefore a function of the whole input and can serve as a fixed-size summary (a sequence embedding) for downstream layers such as a Dense regression head.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This justifies the default return_sequences=False and the typical architecture for the Jena task: an RNN layer followed by a Dense(1) on its last output. It also explains when you do need full sequences: when another RNN layer, or a per-timestep prediction, follows.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 'Contains information about' does not mean 'remembers perfectly': in a SimpleRNN the influence of early inputs fades, which is the vanishing-gradient issue raised on p.393.

terminology.meaning: output_t at the final timestep, shape (output_features,).

connections: p.391: the NumPy RNN that produces successive_outputs
p.393: SimpleRNN struggles to retain long-term dependencies in practice

paragraphs.excerpt: The process you just naively implemented in NumPy corresponds to an actual Keras layer
paragraphs.what_it_says: The NumPy process corresponds to an actual Keras layer, SimpleRNN.
paragraphs.what_it_means: SimpleRNN(units) has the same W, U and b and computes tanh(W·x + U·s + b) at every step (tanh is its default activation), with trainable weights and gradients handled by Keras.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects the from-scratch understanding to the production API.

terminology.meaning: The Keras layer implementing the simple RNN step in a loop over timesteps.

paragraphs.excerpt: There is one minor difference: `SimpleRNN` processes batches of sequences, like all other Keras layers
paragraphs.what_it_says: SimpleRNN processes batches of sequences, taking inputs of shape (batch_size, timesteps, input_features) rather than (timesteps, input_features). In Input(), the timesteps entry can be None to process sequences of arbitrary length.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The batch axis is added in front, and keras.Input's shape argument omits it, so you write shape=(timesteps, features). Writing None for timesteps leaves the length unspecified; the loop simply runs as many steps as the data has. The number of features must still be fixed because it determines the shape of W.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Weights depend only on input_features and units, not on timesteps, which is why one RNN can handle any length. This is a structural advantage over the densely connected model of section 13.2.3 whose first layer size depends on the flattened length.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Within a single batch all sequences must have the same length (a tensor is rectangular); different batches may have different lengths when timesteps is None.

terminology.meaning: Number of sequences processed together; each has its own independent state.
An axis whose size is unknown until data is passed.

connections: p.390: the state is reset between independent sequences such as two samples in a batch
p.384: the dense baseline flattens the sequence and so depends on its length

paragraphs.excerpt: This is especially useful if your model is meant to process sequences of variable length.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Variable length is useful when sequences vary, but if all sequences have the same length, specify the complete input shape: model.summary() then shows output length information, and some performance optimizations become possible (sidebar 'On RNN runtime performance', section 13.3.4).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A fully known shape lets Keras infer all downstream shapes statically and lets the backend compile or unroll the loop more efficiently. A None length forces more generic code.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: For the Jena task, all windows have 120 steps, so shape=(120, 14) is the right choice.

terminology.meaning: Prints each layer's output shape and parameter count.

paragraphs.excerpt: All recurrent layers in Keras (`SimpleRNN`, `LSTM`, and `GRU`) can be run in two different modes
paragraphs.what_it_says: SimpleRNN, LSTM and GRU can return either full sequences of outputs (rank 3, (batch_size, timesteps, output_features)) or only the last output per sequence (rank 2, (batch_size, output_features)), controlled by the return_sequences constructor argument. An example returning only the last output follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: return_sequences=True corresponds to keeping all of successive_outputs in the NumPy code; False corresponds to keeping only the final output_t.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This choice determines what can follow the layer: a Dense head wants the rank-2 last output; another recurrent layer needs the rank-3 sequence (p.393, stacking).

terminology.meaning: Boolean constructor argument; True returns outputs at all timesteps, False (default) only the last.
The units argument of the layer, e.g. 16.

p.628: to stack RNN layers, every layer before the last must return full sequences

concepts.name: Keras SimpleRNN layer
concepts.definition: The Keras layer that implements the simple RNN loop on batches of sequences.
concepts.intuition: The NumPy for loop of p.391, packaged as a trainable layer.
concepts.technical: Input (batch_size, timesteps, input_features); weights W (input_features x units), U (units x units), b (units); output (batch_size, units) or (batch_size, timesteps, units).
concepts.significance: The entry point to recurrent layers in Keras, though rarely used in practice (p.393).
concepts.example: layers.SimpleRNN(16) on 14 features has 14*16 + 16*16 + 16 = 496 parameters (computed, not printed).
concepts.misconception: The timesteps value is not a parameter of the layer; the same layer works for any length.

concepts.name: return_sequences
concepts.definition: Constructor argument of Keras recurrent layers choosing between full output sequences and only the last output.
concepts.intuition: Do you want the network's running commentary, or just its final verdict?
concepts.significance: Required to be True for every recurrent layer that feeds another recurrent layer.
concepts.misconception: return_sequences=False does not discard information computed earlier; the last output depends on the whole sequence through the state.

concepts.name: Variable-length inputs (timesteps=None)
concepts.definition: Declaring the timesteps axis as None in keras.Input so the model accepts sequences of any length.
concepts.intuition: The loop runs as many times as there are elements.
concepts.technical: Possible because RNN weights do not depend on sequence length. Trade-off: less shape information in summary() and fewer optimizations.
concepts.significance: Useful for text or event sequences of varying length.
concepts.misconception: A single batch still needs equal-length sequences; None only allows lengths to differ between calls/batches.

concepts.name: Last output as sequence summary
concepts.definition: The output at the final timestep, which depends on every input timestep.
concepts.intuition: The final state of the scratchpad after reading the whole sequence.
concepts.significance: Allows a fixed-size representation of a variable-length sequence.
concepts.misconception: It is not a perfect memory: older inputs can be attenuated.

code.title: An RNN layer that can process sequences of any length
code.original_code:
num_features = 14
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(None, num_features))
outputs = layers.SimpleRNN(16)(inputs)
code.what_it_does: Declares an input of unknown length with 14 features per step and applies a 16-unit SimpleRNN, returning the last output.

line_explanations.explanation: 14 features, matching the Jena dataset's measurements.
shape=(None, num_features): unspecified timesteps, fixed feature dimension; the batch axis is implicit.
SimpleRNN with 16 units; with the default return_sequences=False the output is (batch_size, 16).

code.algorithm: Loop over however many timesteps the input has.
code.theory_link: Weights depend only on feature count and units, so length can vary.
pitfalls: Assumes `import keras` and `from keras import layers` from earlier in the chapter.
With None length, model.summary() cannot show sequence lengths, and some optimizations are lost.

code.title: An RNN layer that returns only its last output step
code.original_code:
>>> num_features = 14
>>> steps = 120
>>> inputs = keras.Input(shape=(steps, num_features))
>>> outputs = layers.SimpleRNN(16, return_sequences=False)(inputs)
>>> print(outputs.shape)
(None, 16)
code.what_it_does: Applies SimpleRNN(16) to fixed-length sequences of 120 steps and 14 features, returning only the last output; the printed shape is (None, 16).

line_explanations.explanation: return_sequences=False is the default (callout); written explicitly here for clarity.
Output is rank 2: None for the batch axis, 16 units.

code.algorithm: Run 120 recurrent steps, keep only the last output.
code.theory_link: The NOTE: the last output contains information about the whole sequence.

parameters.name: return_sequences
parameters.role: False: return only the last output.

pitfalls: Feeding this rank-2 output into another RNN layer will fail; use return_sequences=True for that (p.393).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written comparison (not from the book)
full = layers.SimpleRNN(16, return_sequences=True)(inputs)
print(full.shape)  # (None, 120, 16)

deeper.title: Mapping NumPy to Keras
deeper.body:
Beyond the book:

| NumPy (p.391) | Keras |
|---|---|
| `inputs` (timesteps, input_features) | input (batch_size, timesteps, input_features) |
| `output_features = 64` | `SimpleRNN(units)` |
| `np.tanh` | default `activation='tanh'` |
| `W`, `U`, `b` | `kernel`, `recurrent_kernel`, `bias` |
| `successive_outputs` | `return_sequences=True` |
| final `output_t` | `return_sequences=False` |

Keras stores `kernel` as (input_features, units), the row-vector convention of the step function on p.391.

deeper.title: When to return full sequences
deeper.body: Beyond the book: return the full sequence when (1) another recurrent layer follows (stacking, p.393), (2) you need a prediction at every timestep (e.g. tagging each token), or (3) an attention or pooling layer will look across all timesteps. Return only the last output when a single prediction per sequence is needed, as in the Jena forecast.

takeaways: Each output of an RNN carries information about all previous inputs, so the last output often suffices.
Keras recurrent layers take (batch_size, timesteps, input_features).
timesteps=None in keras.Input allows arbitrary-length sequences; use a full shape when lengths are fixed.
return_sequences=True gives (batch_size, timesteps, units); False (default) gives (batch_size, units).

questions.question: What is the output shape of layers.SimpleRNN(16) applied to keras.Input(shape=(120, 14)) with default arguments?
questions.explanation: return_sequences=False is the default, so only the last output (16 units) is returned with a batch axis of None. (None, 120, 16) is the return_sequences=True shape; (120, 16) omits the batch axis; 14 is the input feature count.

questions.question: How do you allow a Keras RNN model to process sequences of arbitrary length?
questions.answer: Set the timesteps entry of keras.Input's shape to None, e.g. keras.Input(shape=(None, num_features)).

questions.question: Why can the last output of an RNN be used as a summary of the entire sequence?
questions.answer: Because each output at timestep t depends on inputs 0..t through the recurrent state, so the last output depends on the whole sequence.
questions.explanation: This is the NOTE at the top of the page.

questions.question: Give two reasons from the page to specify a complete input shape when all sequences have the same length.
questions.answer: model.summary() can display output length information, and it can unlock performance optimizations.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after Listing 13.16, with a pointer to the runtime-performance sidebar.

questions.question: Which recurrent layers support return_sequences, according to the page?
options: None; it is a model-level option
questions.explanation: The page says all recurrent layers in Keras (SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU) can run in the two modes, controlled by the return_sequences constructor argument. It is a layer argument, not a model option.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does SimpleRNN(16) have on inputs with 14 features?
questions.explanation: Kernel W (14 x 16), recurrent kernel U (16 x 16), bias (16), following the W, U, b parameterization of p.390. The count is independent of the 120 timesteps.

questions.question: Can you say, for a model consisting of two stacked SimpleRNN layers and a Dense(1) head, which return_sequences value each RNN needs?
questions.answer: The first RNN needs return_sequences=True (the next RNN needs a sequence); the second can use the default False so Dense(1) receives a rank-2 tensor.
questions.explanation: Follows from the two modes on this page; the stacking listing is on p.393.
